subject: africanElephant
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: adult African bush elephant.
Style: low-poly.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module to build a low-poly stylized elephant using the SDK's builder API—joints, chains, sweeps, parts, sticks, surfaces, painting, and texture effects like mottle, grain, and countershading—while keeping complexity manageable and scaling to realistic African bush elephant proportions.

I'm setting up the shoulder height around 3 meters with proportional body length, importing the builder's path and paint utilities, then laying out the skeleton starting from a pelvis joint and building a spine chain with positioned keyframe points running from hips toward the chest.

Next I'm planning the neck and head joint placement, then defining the body as a swept barrel shape along the spine chain with a radius function that varies from narrower at the hips to wider at the belly.

I'm also working out the four leg attachments—shoulder joint positions, foot targets, and limb segment lengths needed to reach the ground properly.

I'll simplify and just use [0,0,1] for front legs and [0,0,-1] for hind legs following the digitigrade pattern, placing hind hips and foot targets symmetrically on each side. For the chain structure, I'm working out that a limb with 3 joint points needs 3 names corresponding to the 2 spans plus the tip.

To be safe I'll settle on 2-segment limbs for both front and hind legs, with lengths like [1.25, 1.1] for the front, naming each chain by joint (shoulder, elbow, wrist) so 2 spans plus 1 tip gives the 3 required names.

For the foot, I'm sculpting a short, slightly tapered cylinder (wider at bottom than top) attached at the wrist bone, positioned so its bottom edge roughly touches the ground plane.

For the limbs, I'm planning a sweep function that follows the bone chain with a tapering radius, thicker at the top of the limb and narrowing toward the end, then building a named chain for each leg that attaches to the hips with defined joint points.

I'm now setting up the spine chain rooted at the pelvis, dividing it into three named spans so I can reference chest and back joints separately, then attaching the front legs to the chest joint and hind legs to the pelvis, defining the actual spine path coordinates from pelvis up through the back.

Checking the body proportions, though—with belly radius 0.85 the back would hit 3.35m, taller than a real elephant's ~3.1m shoulder height, so I'm lowering the spine's y-position and shifting the belly down to compensate, then working out where the legs need to sit so their tops meet the adjusted body bottom.

Now I'm placing shoulder and hip joints inside the body volume and computing leg root/foot distances to verify the segment lengths can actually span the gap—front legs rooted near the chest at roughly (0.5, 2.1, 0.5) reaching down to the foot near (0.5, 0.15, 0.55), and hind legs rooted around (0.5, 2.0, -0.9) reaching to (0.5, 0.15, -0.9), both checking out against the chosen segment lengths.

I'm also working out the neck and head rig: building a short catmull-rom chain from the chest joint up to a point near the head, then attaching the head as a joint parented to the neck's last segment, making sure the aim/orientation vectors point forward and up naturally.

For the head mesh, I'm sculpting a skull using a scaled sphere geometry for the basic shape, then planning the ears as separate extruded flat shapes positioned at the sides of the head to give that big fan-eared look.

Still writing ear geometry...

Working out the mirroring for the ear pair, noting the thickness extrusion direction stays consistent while the lateral x-offset flips sign for the mirrored side.

Good, the ear position works with that offset. Now for the tusks, I'm sweeping a bezier curve from base to tip with a tapering radius, attached to the head bone with ivory coloring.

Working out the tusk geometry: the base sits low on the front sides of the head, with control points pulling forward and then curving up-outward toward the tip, using a cubic bezier through four points.

Now I'm plotting the trunk as a chain hanging from the lower front of the head, curling downward and defining a sequence of points to shape its curve.

Defining the trunk chain...

Skipping the nostril detail for simplicity. For eyes, I'll place small dark spheres with a tiny white highlight near the head position. For the tail, I'm planning a chain sweeping back and down from the pelvis through a few path points.

Building tail geometry...

Defining color palette...

Adding hind toe nails, then checking skeleton naming for uniqueness across limb joints and verifying the spine chain parents correctly to the pelvis root. Now I'm setting up the body sweep along the spine using a radius function to shape the torso.

I'm scaling the body proportions to match a real 3-meter shoulder height elephant, adjusting the body length and head position so the overall silhouette stays anatomically plausible.

Lowering the head center to 2.75 with a smaller vertical radius so the top caps around 3.15 instead of overshooting. Now I'm working out the neck joint chain connecting the chest to the head, tracing where the spine path ends so the neck segments flow naturally into the head position.

Continuing on, I'm defining the spine path points and assigning joint names, then placing the chest joint at the third spine point. I'm also setting the front and hind limb roots relative to spine joints, noticing the hind root position sits a bit off from the corresponding spine joint and needs adjusting.

Now I'm naming the limb joints -- shoulder/elbow/wrist for front legs and hip/knee/ankle for hind legs -- and checking segment lengths against root-to-target distances to make sure they're plausible. I'm setting up the limb function calls with bend directions and building the joint chains with proper parent references.

I'm sweeping each leg chain with a tapering radius from thigh to ankle, verifying the foot lands close enough to the ground pad, and sizing the round foot pad cylinder to cover the ankle base. Then I'm moving to the ears, planning an extruded outline with enough points and smoothing for a thin, rounded shape.

Working out the ear's thickness taper and checking its placement on the head so it sits on the surface slightly outward from the head's width, oriented correctly for mirroring to the other side.

Adjusting the eye position so it sits just inside the head radius, moving forward to 0.42 with a small sphere size, checking visibility from the front.

Using 0.05 radius eye spheres positioned relative to the head joint, then setting up the head sphere anchored at the head joint's local origin with its own scale. Now I'm planning the trunk as a chain parented to the head, starting from a point offset down and forward from the head, defined through a series of catmull-rom points.

Writing trunk sweep code...

I'll skip detailed wrinkle rings and nostril discs for simplicity, focusing instead on the tusks—sweeping a bezier curve with four points off the head's local coordinates, tapering the radius from thick to a pointed tip with flat start caps.

Now I'm adding the tail as a chain hanging from the pelvis joint, using a catmull curve through four points with a sweep that tapers thinner toward the end, plus a small dark tuft sphere attached near the tip. I'm also defining the hide color using a countershade/mottle combination, with ivory for the tusks.

Setting nail, eye, and ear tones separately, with the ears given a flat grayish-pink hue. I'm deciding to skip extra details like wrinkles, forehead dome, eyelid, and mouth to keep things moderate, and double-checking that the sweep function's radius argument is correctly shaped as a function of t.

Working out the body radius function so the spine widens appropriately toward the chest and rump, settling on sine-based rx/ry formulas, then confirming the resulting body height lines up reasonably and that the sweep will correctly use the chain's default joints.

Now I'm setting up the trunk's root attachment at the head and writing the import statements, checking that all needed builder functions (bezier, catmull, limb, mottle, countershade, grain, paint) are properly exported from the single module and trimming unused imports like rng. I'm starting to define the builder instance and sketch out the main build function structure.

Defining hide, ear, ivory, ink, and foot color palettes...

Setting up the pelvis joint as the root of the skeleton, deciding whether to specify an aim direction for the spine chain or leave default orientation.

Building the spine chain from the pelvis using a catmull-rom curve through four points, splitting it into three named segments with a "spine" role. Then sweeping a body shape along the spine with a radius function that bulges slightly using sine curves for both x and y, hiding the color and rounding the end caps.

Next I'm constructing the neck as its own chain parented to the last spine joint, tapering its radius down toward the head, then placing the head joint with an aim target slightly forward and up to orient it. I'm adding a sphere geometry for the head skull, attaching it to the head bone at the head's position with a slightly flattened, elongated scale to approximate skull shape.

Writing more head features...

Still writing the trunk curve...

I'm verifying the trunk's starting offset from the head position works out correctly, computing that the downward and forward shifts land it at the right coordinates before continuing into the trunk point.

Now I'm sketching the trunk sweep, tapering its radius from base to tip, and deciding to skip finer details like nostril shaping and wrinkle rings for simplicity. Moving on, I'm starting to set up the leg positions using a side-multiplier array for mirroring left and right.

Building out the front leg chains...

Adding toenail geometry...

I'm now setting up the hind limb chain with hip, knee, and foot positions and a backward-pointing bend direction.

Placing three toenails near the front of the hind foot, then setting up the hind limb as a straight vertical chain with a knee bend from hip to foot. For the tail, I'm building a curved catmull-rom chain off the pelvis with tapering sweep radius and hide coloring, plus adding a tuft sphere at the end.

Now I'm designing the ear shape as a 2D outline extruded with thickness and smoothing, colored and attached to the head bone, positioning it so the proportions feel stylized-elephant-sized relative to the skull.

I'm double-checking foot cylinder placement so the bottom sits flush at ground level, and verifying leg roots and spine curvature keep everything tucked inside the body silhouette without clipping. Considering whether to add a belly shape before finalizing and returning the root.
